lesson.title: Where Does the Missing Power Go: Grading a Circuit's Efficiency
lesson.summary: Efficiency compares real power delivered to a load against real power drawn from the source, and the gap between them is heat lost in resistive elements along the way.
lesson.body:
Power tells you the rate energy moves through a circuit, and Real Power specifically tells you the rate energy is actually consumed or delivered to useful work, as opposed to the reactive power that merely sloshes back and forth without being spent. Efficiency takes those two ideas and asks a very practical question: of all the real power a source supplies, how much actually reaches the load doing useful work, and how much is lost as heat along the way.

The formula is simple in form, efficiency = Pout / Pin, usually expressed as a percentage by multiplying by 100. Pin is the real power drawn from the source, and Pout is the real power delivered to the load, whatever that load happens to be, a motor, a speaker, a downstream circuit board. The difference, Pin minus Pout, has to go somewhere, and in almost every real circuit it goes into heat dissipated by the resistive parts of the system, wire resistance, transformer winding resistance, switching losses in a converter, and so on. Efficiency is never greater than 100 percent for a passive or lossy system, because you cannot get more real power out than you put in.

Here is a worked example. Consider a small DC to DC converter that draws Pin = 120 W from its input source and delivers Pout = 102 W to its load. The efficiency is Pout / Pin times 100 = (102/120) times 100 = 0.85 times 100 = 85 percent. The power lost as heat inside the converter is Pin minus Pout = 120 minus 102 = 18 W, and that 18 W is exactly what a thermal engineer would need to account for when choosing a heat sink or enclosure. Notice the arithmetic checks both ways, 85 percent of 120 W is 102 W, and 102 plus 18 equals 120, so the energy balance closes.

Efficiency calculations apply just as naturally to AC systems, where Pin and Pout are both real power figures measured in watts, never the apparent power in volt amps and never the reactive power in VAR. This is an important distinction, because a circuit can move enormous apparent power back and forth between a source and a reactive load, as seen in Power in Capacitors and Power in Inductors, without that reactive flow counting against efficiency at all, since reactive power is not consumed in the first place. Only the resistive losses, the genuinely dissipated real power, subtract from the numerator.

In practice, efficiency is one of the first numbers engineers quote when comparing designs, because it converts abstract watts into a single comparable percentage. A power supply rated at 92 percent efficiency wastes noticeably less energy as heat, and therefore needs less cooling and costs less to run, than one rated at 80 percent, even if both deliver the same output power to the load. Chasing higher efficiency, by reducing resistive losses wherever current flows, is one of the most persistent themes in circuit design, from household chargers up to power grid transformers.
